dialogue.l27_briefing.line1: Three teams brought me claims this week, all backed by strong-looking numbers, all asking for budget.
dialogue.l27_briefing.line2: I need someone to actually cross-examine these before I sign off.
dialogue.l27_briefing.line3: Then let's treat each one like a case - the numbers might be real, but that doesn't mean the story attached to them is.
dialogue.l27_investigation.line1: Every one of these correlations is real - nobody's making up the numbers.
dialogue.l27_investigation.line2: The question is who ended up in each group, and whether that alone explains the gap.
dialogue.l27_investigation.line3: Sustain the objection if the comparison doesn't hold up. Overrule it if it does.
dialogue.l27_independent_intro.line1: Same three cases, no hints this time.
dialogue.l27_twist.line1: NovaMart once had an opt-in checkout beta that looked like a massive win.
dialogue.l27_twist.line2: Here's what a real randomized test found once nobody could self-select anymore.
dialogue.l27_debrief.line1: So the real effect was a fraction of what the beta numbers suggested.
dialogue.l27_debrief.line2: Every case today had the same shape - a real gap, and a group that got there on its own.
dialogue.l27_debrief.line3: A verdict without a proper comparison group is just a good story wearing a number.
lesson.l28.title: Chart Crime Lab
lesson.l28.objective1: Recognize when a chart's axis, window, or denominator is doing the persuading
lesson.l28.objective2: Redraw a chart so its visual impression matches its real numbers
lesson.l28.objective3: Approve, reject, or redesign a chart and explain why
lesson.l28.request.satisfaction_score_cl: Customer satisfaction rose from 72 to 75 this year. Leadership wants a chart that makes the improvement land.
A real 3-point gain can be drawn to look like almost anything, depending on where the axis starts.
lesson.l28.request.active_users_claim.pr: Someone wants a chart of monthly active users for the year-end deck.
lesson.l28.request.active_users_claim.hi: Check what the months you're not showing actually did.
lesson.l28.request.returns_rate_claim.pr: The ops team wants a chart of the product return rate by quarter.
lesson.l28.request.returns_rate_claim.hi: Ask what a return rate should actually be measured against.
lesson.l28.twist_spend_change_label: Marketing spend, change over the year
lesson.l28.field.chart_review_standard.p: What's the right standard for approving a chart before it goes out?
lesson.l28.field.chart_review_standard.h: Think about what made the dual-axis chart misleading despite correct numbers.
Numbers and visuals both must be honest
Only the written report needs to be accurate
lesson.l28.field.general_lesson.prompt: What's the general lesson from today?
lesson.l28.field.general_lesson.hint: Think about what stayed the same across every flawed chart today.
lesson.l28.option.general_lesson.same_da: The same data looks different sliced
lesson.l28.option.general_lesson.dual_ax: Dual-axis charts are always the right choice
dialogue.l28_briefing.line1: Marketing keeps sending me charts to double-check before they go out, and something feels off about a few of them.
dialogue.l28_briefing.line2: The numbers all check out - it's something about how they're drawn.
dialogue.l28_briefing.line3: That's the actual crime scene here. A chart can be completely honest about its numbers and still mislead everyone who looks at it.
dialogue.l28_investigation.line1: Same real data every time - only how it's scaled, windowed, or divided changes.
dialogue.l28_investigation.line2: A truncated axis, a cherry-picked date range, and the wrong denominator all do the same job: make a real number tell a different story.
dialogue.l28_investigation.line3: Pick the version you'd actually publish.
dialogue.l28_independent_intro.line1: Same three charts, no hints this time.

dialogue.l28_debrief.line1: So the dual-axis chart wasn't wrong about a single number.
dialogue.l28_debrief.line2: It didn't have to be. Choosing the scale was the whole trick.
dialogue.l28_debrief.line3: A chart earns approval by being honest twice - once in its numbers, once in how it shows them.
lesson.l29.title: The Executive Brief
lesson.l29.objective1: Tell a decision-relevant finding apart from a merely dramatic one
lesson.l29.objective2: Select findings, evidence, and a recommendation that actually fit together
lesson.l29.objective3: Deliver a brief that's accurate, useful, and appropriately cautious

dialogue.l29_briefing.line1: The board wants three minutes on the checkout redesign, not thirty slides. Give me the brief.

handbook.article.asking_an_analytical_qu: A stakeholder asks a question that sounds perfectly clear until you try to answer it. "Are customers becoming less loyal?" has an obvious-sounding yes-or-no shape, but nothing about the sentence says which customers, over what period, based on what behavior, or what "loyal" is even supposed to mean. That gap, between a question that sounds answerable and a question a dataset can actually answer, is where a surprising amount of bad analysis starts - not in the numbers themselves.

The reason a vague question survives this long is that it doesn't feel vague from the inside. "Less loyal" already conjures a specific mental picture for whoever asked it - probably repeat purchases, or maybe app opens, or maybe just a gut sense that something's off. The trouble is that everyone who hears the question fills in their own picture, and two people can walk away agreeing to "check if customers are less loyal" while meaning two different measurable things. An analytical question is one where that filling-in has already happened on paper: who's being counted, over what window, based on what specific behavior, and against what earlier baseline.

Turning a vague ask into an analytical one usually means pinning down the same handful of things every time: which unit you're actually counting (an order? a customer? a session?), over what stretch of time, within which slice of the population, against which specific metric, and - easy to forget - what decision the answer is actually going to inform. That last one matters more than it looks: a number can be perfectly correct and still useless if nobody can say what changes depending on whether it comes back high or low.

Being this specific has a real cost, and it's worth naming rather than pretending precision is free. A question pinned down too early can blind you to the thing actually worth finding: if "loyal" gets defined as "made a second purchase within 30 days" before anyone's looked at the data, a genuinely different and more interesting pattern (say, a huge drop specifically among customers who contacted support) can sail right past unnoticed, because nobody was looking for it. The fix isn't to stay vague; it's to treat the first specific version of the question as a working draft, not a locked contract, specific enough to start analyzing and loose enough to revise once the data actually starts talking back.

None of this guarantees the question is the right one to be asking in the first place. A perfectly well-specified brief can still measure something that doesn't actually matter to the business, or answer a narrower version of the real concern behind it. Sharpening a question makes it operationalized and answerable with data; it doesn't make it wise. That judgment (is this even the question worth spending the week on) stays a human call no amount of structure replaces.
handbook.article.observation_unit_and_gr: Two questions shape a dataset more than most people realize, and both get skipped more often than they should: what, exactly, does one row represent, and at what level of detail was it recorded? The first is what this course calls the observation unit; the second is the grain. In practice the two ideas often overlap, and the sharp line drawn between them here is a teaching simplification, not a strict rule the rest of the industry follows. Neither shows up as a labeled column anywhere - they're properties of the table as a whole, and getting them wrong doesn't usually throw an error. It just quietly produces a number that means something other than what everyone assumes it means.

The observation unit is the thing you're counting - the unit you'd point to and say "that's one." An order is one thing; a customer is another; a single line item inside an order is a third, even though all three might live in tables that look superficially similar. NovaMart's own analytical brief makes this an explicit, unavoidable first choice for exactly this reason: before anyone can argue about whether a number is high or low, everyone answering the question has to be counting the same kind of thing.

Grain is the related but separate question of how fine or coarse that counting actually is - whether a row represents one order, one order line, one customer-day, or one customer-month. A revenue table can honestly claim to be "per order" and still hide a real problem if what's actually needed is "per order line," because a single order with three products would already be summed into one number before anyone gets a chance to look at the products separately.

Grain mismatches are dangerous specifically because they don't announce themselves. Summing a column that's actually recorded at a finer grain than you think produces a real number, one that runs without complaint through every downstream calculation - it's just the wrong number, inflated or deflated by however many extra rows each real-world entity happened to contribute. The fix isn't a special check for this one failure mode; it's asking, before writing a single line of aggregation code, "what does one row in this table actually represent" and confirming the answer out loud rather than assuming it matches whatever the column names suggest.

Choosing a grain is also a real trade-off, not just a fact to get right. Finer-grained data often makes it possible to build a coarser view later, as long as the dimensions and raw measures that view will need were actually kept and the aggregation itself is done correctly - simply summing values that are already averages, rates, or unique counts produces a wrong number, not just a less detailed one. Finer data is also heavier to store, slower to query, and easier to draw a wrong conclusion from if someone aggregates it incorrectly. Coarser data is lighter and faster, but it locks in a specific view of the world at collection time.

That limit plays out differently depending on what's actually being aggregated. Revenue is additive, so a table stored "per day" sums correctly into "per month": each day's total is a real piece of the month's total. A daily conversion rate is different: a simple average of daily conversion rates is not generally the true multi-day rate, because days rarely have the same number of eligible sessions, and an unweighted average silently treats them as if they did. It's still possible to recompute the rate correctly at a coarser grain without ever touching raw events, as long as its two components (conversions and eligible sessions) were both kept and summed on their own - dividing the summed conversions by the summed eligible sessions gives the true multi-day rate, equivalent to weighting each day's rate by that day's own session count rather than averaging the percentages directly. The rate itself doesn't need to be additive if what it's built from is. Daily unique users is the harder case. Knowing 500 people were active Monday and 500 Tuesday says nothing about whether they were the same 500 or 1,000 different ones, and no amount of correctly-kept daily counts can answer that; a real monthly figure needs the underlying identity information, not just more detailed sums. When there's real doubt about what a future question might need, the safer default is keeping data finer, and keeping the specific components a rate is built from rather than just the rate itself.
handbook.article.metrics_need_definition: Two teams can each pull "active users" for the exact same week, using the exact same underlying event log, and walk away with two different numbers - and neither team made a mistake. "Active" sounds like a fact about a user until you notice it was never actually specified: active by opening the app once? By completing an action? Within the last day, the last 7, the last 30? Every one of those is a defensible reading of the word, and every one produces a different count from the same raw data.

This isn't a data-quality problem in the usual sense - the events themselves can be perfectly clean and complete. The gap lives entirely in the metric's own definition, or lack of one. A metric name is a promise to measure something specific; until someone writes down exactly which action, over exactly which window, counted exactly how (once per user? once per session? every occurrence?), the name is doing more work than the definition actually supports.

Tightening a loose definition always trades away something. A stricter "active" (say, completing a specific in-app action rather than merely opening it) excludes behavior that a looser definition would have counted, and that's not a flaw to apologize for: it's the price of the number meaning the same thing to everyone who reads it. Which definition is "right" isn't something the data can settle by itself - it depends on which construct the number is actually meant to represent. The alternative, leaving "active" comfortably vague, keeps every reader free to imagine their own favorable interpretation, which is a worse trade the moment the number has to justify a real decision rather than just describe a vague trend.

A written-down definition isn't a permanent fix, either. It has a shelf life tied to whatever the product actually does: the moment NovaMart ships a feature that changes what "using the app" even means - a new passive notification that technically opens a session without anyone touching anything, say - yesterday's careful definition of "active" can start quietly measuring the wrong thing again, precisely because nobody thought to revisit it. A metric definition is something to maintain, not something to write once and trust forever.
handbook.article.time_windows_change_ans: The same NovaMart metric, pulled the same afternoon by the same person, can show a 4-point improvement or a 2-point decline depending on nothing but which stretch of time it's measured against. Both computations can be arithmetically correct; they don't have to be equally appropriate answers to the actual question being asked. Two different, unstated questions happened to get asked using the same words.

An analytical brief's timeframe field forces one specific window into the open for a single question - this metric, this period, full stop. The broader pattern this article is actually about is what happens across many questions: any time a result is compared against "before," the choice of how far back "before" reaches is doing real, silent work on the answer, whether or not anyone wrote it down as a formal timeframe.

A short window is responsive - it reflects a recent change quickly - but it's also noisy, prone to making an ordinary bad week look like a trend and an ordinary good week look like a breakthrough. A long window smooths that noise out, but it's slow to notice a real, recent shift, and it can bury a genuine two-week problem inside twelve months of otherwise-fine numbers.

Neither length is generically correct; the right one depends on what the number is actually for. A metric feeding a same-day operational alert needs a short window almost by definition - waiting a quarter to confirm a real outage defeats the point of alerting at all. A metric feeding an annual strategic decision needs enough history to separate a real shift from ordinary week-to-week noise, and a short window there risks reacting to something that would have resolved itself by next month.

Even a well-chosen window doesn't settle the question by itself, and a window shouldn't be picked only after seeing which one produces the preferred answer - that's cherry-picking a result, not choosing a methodology. Two honestly-chosen windows can still disagree, and when they do, the disagreement itself is information: it can point to real seasonality, an underlying trend, a genuine shift in conditions, or a baseline that's moved - not necessarily to one window being secretly the "real" one and the other wrong. Always state which window a number came from, and treat any switch between windows as a methodological decision that needs a real justification, not a silent default.
handbook.article.schema_is_a_contract.bo: A shipment record in NovaMart's fulfillment export carries a column called shipment_id, and every value in it is a plain integer: 100042, 100043, and so on. Nothing about that column's dtype raises a flag - int64 is exactly what a well-behaved numeric column looks like. And yet running shipment_id.mean() is perfectly legal code that answers a question nobody asked. The number it produces is real and computable, and completely meaningless, because shipment_id was never a quantity to begin with. It's a label wearing a number's clothing.

That's the gap between a column's physical representation and its semantic type, and a dtype only ever answers the first question. Sometimes pandas infers that dtype from the raw bytes; sometimes a loader is told it explicitly - dtype=, parse_dates=, a declared schema - so a column's physical type can be a deliberate choice, not just a guess. Neither path touches the second question. A semantic type is a much larger, open-ended judgment: identifier, timestamp, currency, duration, category, a genuine measurement. Whether a number is a quantity or a label is a fact about the business behind the data, not about how carefully its bytes were typed.

The more dangerous version of this gap doesn't even announce itself with a wrong-looking dtype. A column can already be exactly the type it should be, a clean float64, and still be wrong, because the unit or convention behind those numbers quietly changed for part of the data. Picture a delivery-duration column that switches from minutes to seconds for one source system after an unflagged migration: no parse error, no missing value, every row still a valid number. The computation runs, returns a plausible-looking figure, and measures the wrong thing for however many rows came from that one source - a failure a dtype check will never catch, because there's nothing in it for a dtype check to catch.

What actually resolves both cases is the same thing: a data contract, an explicit statement of what a column means, what unit or format it's in, and which operations on it are legitimate - going beyond anything a dtype alone can express. A contract isn't something a dataset carries automatically. It's an agreement between whoever produces a column and whoever consumes it, and like any agreement between two systems, it can go stale the moment one side changes without telling the other. A new source system, a redefined field, a migration nobody thought to flag in the analysis itself - none of these need to touch a single dtype to break the contract underneath it.

None of this makes df.dtypes useless. It's still the fastest way to spot the columns that are obviously wrong: identifiers stored with stray punctuation, dates still sitting in a string column. What it can't do is vouch for a column that already shows the "right" dtype, because rightness at that level was never the question a contract actually answers. Ask a second question of every column that matters to the result, every time: not just what type is this, but what is it supposed to mean, and does what actually arrived still match that.
handbook.article.missingness_has_a_mecha: A picking record in NovaMart Go's fulfillment export carries a column called pick_minutes, and for 14% of this period's orders, it's simply blank. Dropping those rows and reading the SLA rate off what's left produces a clean, plausible-looking number that clears the target with room to spare. Nothing about that number announces a problem - it's a real computation on real rows, and it's still the wrong answer, because the rows that dropped out aren't a random slice of the ones that stayed.

Missingness concentrated in one segment - here, orders picked on legacy handheld scanners during the evening rush - is a real, provable fact: group the data by scanner and hour, and the gap in how often pick_minutes goes missing is right there in the numbers. What that fact doesn't prove is why those particular gaps exist. A statistician would call the underlying process a missingness mechanism - MCAR, missing completely at random; MAR, where missingness no longer depends on the missing value itself once you condition on what's observed; MNAR, where that dependence can remain even after conditioning on everything observed. All three sound like something a table could confirm. None of them can be, not from the table alone.

What the data can show is an association: the missing rate genuinely differs by scanner and by hour, a fact about observed variables. What it cannot show, from the data alone, is the value the completion scan would have recorded had it fired - whether a slow pick lost its scan more often than a fast one, in exactly the way that would bias a naive average. Device logs and provenance notes can make that mechanism more or less plausible. Believing it, and being able to prove it directly from the rows in front of you, are different things - and a real analysis says which one it's doing.

The honest response isn't to guess a value and move on. Given how many rows are missing and what the observed ones show, two extreme assumptions - every missing pick failed the SLA, or every missing pick passed it - bound the real answer without requiring the mechanism to be known at all. When that range comfortably clears a decision threshold either way, the missing data doesn't matter to the decision. When it straddles the threshold, the visible data genuinely doesn't resolve the question, no matter how confident a single filled-in number looks.

Not every blank cell is the same kind of blank, either. A column that's missing because an event went uncaptured, a column that's missing because the thing it measures never existed for that row, and a column whose missing value is itself the real answer - fillna() treats all three identically, and only one of them was ever a measurement problem to begin with. The right treatment follows from what the gap actually means, not from a single rule applied to every NaN in the frame.
handbook.article.duplicates_need_an_iden: NovaMart Pay's payment-event feed came in twice after a redelivery incident, and a first pass with duplicated().sum() finds a handful of exact repeats worth removing. That check answers one specific question - are any two rows byte-for-byte identical - and nothing about a payment feed guarantees that's the question worth answering. A webhook replay of the same event, two lifecycle stages of the same payment, two attempts at the same order, and two genuinely separate purchases can all sit in the same table, sharing some column or another, and only one of those four is actually a duplicate of anything.

A shared value doesn't make two rows duplicates until a key is named. Two rows sharing an order ID might be two lifecycle events of one payment, or two entirely separate attempts after a decline - both real, neither a duplicate of the other, and a dedupe keyed on order ID alone would silently destroy whichever one it decided not to keep. The identity that actually matters - an event, a payment attempt, an order - has to be chosen on purpose, against the question being asked, not assumed from whichever column happens to repeat.

duplicated() with no key can also miss the real problem entirely. Two rows that share an event ID but disagree on the recorded amount are not row-identical, so a bare full-row check doesn't even flag them - the exact case a naive cleanup pass walks straight past while congratulating itself on a clean-looking number. Checking a real business key, and checking whether the values under it actually agree, are two different questions, and the second one is usually the one that finds the real damage.

Once a key is chosen, keep='first' or keep='last' decides which row survives - and that choice is a tie-break, not a policy. When both surviving candidates report the same fact, which one is kept genuinely doesn't matter. When they disagree, keeping whichever one happened to load first is a real decision made by row order, silently, with no one having actually decided anything.

A real conflict - the same identity, two disagreeing records - doesn't always have a safe automatic answer. Picking one value and moving on hides the disagreement instead of resolving it; the honest response is often to set the conflicting value aside, say so in the reported number, and let it be reconciled at the source. That doesn't mean discarding everything the two records agree on: if a captured payment's own status and IDs are identical between both copies and only the amount disagrees, the order is still confirmed captured - only its exact amount is unresolved, so a report can say exactly that instead of quietly treating the whole record as excluded. That's a different question from the one an article on observation unit and grain already answers: grain says what one row is supposed to represent, and this is about verifying whether two actual rows are honestly the same occurrence of it.
handbook.article.outlier_is_a_flag_not_a: Outlier Is a Flag, Not a Verdict

NovaMart Logistics' own fulfillment-cost feed has a handful of orders sitting far from the rest - a quick screen (a fence around the middle of the distribution, or any similar heuristic) flags every one of them in seconds. That screen answers exactly one question: which rows sit unusually far from the center. It says nothing about why, and why is what actually decides what happens next. Four real orders can trip the same flag for four completely different reasons - and only one of those reasons is an actual error.

One of those reasons is a genuine data-entry error - a decimal or unit slip that produced a number nobody actually charged or paid. Correcting it is the right call, but only when something real grounds the specific correction: an invoice, a source log, a contract note stating the actual value. 'This number looks too big, so it probably meant something smaller' is a guess dressed up as a correction - without a real source to correct to, the honest move is to flag the row for investigation, not invent a value that merely looks more plausible.

A second reason is a real, legitimate observation that just happens to be rare - an enterprise order at ten times the usual size, correctly recorded, correctly charged. Nothing about it needs fixing. What it might need is scoping: a metric asking what a typical standard order costs has a real reason to set it aside, but that reason has to come from what the order actually is - a real business-metadata field, a contract type, an account tier - never from how far its own value sits from the middle of the distribution. Excluding it because it looks too big is exactly the same unfounded move as correcting the data-entry error without a real source; excluding it because it's genuinely a different kind of order is a real, defensible population decision. Scoping it out of one metric doesn't mean discarding it - a total-exposure figure still has to include every real dollar actually spent, the rare order included.

A third reason isn't about any single row at all - it's about which population a whole group of rows actually belongs to. A single global fence, built from every order at once, can flag an entire legitimate segment simply because that segment's own normal range sits higher than everyone else's - a remote-zone delivery surcharge, a same-day rush fee, a category with its own real cost structure. Judged against everyone else, every one of those orders looks extreme. Judged against its own segment's own distribution, none of them do. The fix isn't a bigger fence - it's checking whether the flagged rows share something that changes what normal means for them specifically, before assuming the fence itself is telling the truth.

A fourth reason is the one screening exists to actually find: a real, correctly recorded event that's genuinely unusual because something real happened - an outage, an incident, a real disruption worth knowing about. That row isn't a data problem at all; deleting it or quietly smoothing it away doesn't clean the data, it erases the one fact most worth keeping. The right move is to keep it and name what it is. Every one of these four cases comes back to the same real question, the one an article on observation unit and grain and the glossary's own definition of population both point toward: does this observation belong to the population the question is actually about, and does the data itself - not how far the number sits from the middle - say so? A flag is where to look. It was never the answer.
handbook.glossary.analytical_question.de: A business question rewritten precisely enough to check against data: which unit is being counted, over what timeframe, within which population, against which specific metric, and for what decision. A vague question ("are customers less loyal?") can sound answerable while actually meaning several different measurable things at once. See "Asking an Analytical Question" for the trade-offs involved in getting this specific.
handbook.glossary.observation_unit.defin: The specific thing a dataset counts one row of - an order, a customer, a single line item - even when several of these look similar at a glance. Getting this wrong doesn't crash anything; it just means two people can compute a "correct" number about two different kinds of things without noticing.
handbook.glossary.grain.definition: How fine or coarse a dataset's own rows are recorded: a table can track a customer overall, a customer per day, or a customer per product per day - each a valid but different grain for describing "the same" customer. In practice, observation unit and grain often overlap; this course's sharp distinction between them is a teaching simplification, not a strict industry-wide rule. Also seen called "granularity" outside this course.
handbook.glossary.metric_definition.defi: The exact, written-down rule behind a metric's name: which action counts, over what window, counted how many times per user. A metric name alone ("active users") is a promise a definition has to actually keep - without one, two teams computing "the same" metric can honestly disagree.
handbook.glossary.time_window.definition: The span of time a result is actually computed or compared over - last 7 days, last quarter, year over year. The same metric can show improvement or decline depending only on which window it's read through; both readings can be arithmetically correct without being equally appropriate answers to the question being asked. Distinct, in this course's own terminology, from Timeframe - the specific brief field naming one fixed window for a single analytical question. In everyday use the two words are often interchangeable; the distinction here is a deliberate teaching convention, not a universal rule.
handbook.glossary.timeframe.definition: The specific time period named in an analytical brief for one particular question - a fixed input, not a general concept. See Time Window for the broader idea that different window choices can change a result even outside a formal brief. This course draws a deliberate line between the two terms as a teaching convention; general usage doesn't always keep them this separate.
handbook.glossary.population.definition: The full group a question is actually about, before any sampling or filtering happens - all NovaMart customers, or specifically all customers in one market. Naming the population precisely matters as much as naming the metric: a true statement about one slice can be silently misread as a claim about everyone.
handbook.glossary.sample.definition: A subset of a population actually examined, used to say something about the whole without checking every member. How that subset gets chosen (see Sampling) determines whether conclusions drawn from it can honestly generalize back to the full population.
handbook.glossary.sampling.definition: The method used to choose which members of a population end up in a sample. A biased method - even one applied perfectly consistently - can produce a sample that looks representative and isn't. This course's own Sampling Mission lesson explores exactly this problem in depth.
handbook.glossary.confounder.definition: A third factor that influences both sides of an apparent relationship, making two things look connected when the real cause is something else entirely. A real correlation can be completely genuine and still not mean what it first appears to, once a confounder is accounted for.
